prize_parts.citation: for foundational theoretical and computational discoveries on collective motion and the hydrodynamics of active matter

statement.case_for: Active-matter hydrodynamics created a new branch of nonequilibrium statistical physics. Vicsek's minimal flocking model showed that collective motion is a genuine nonequilibrium phase transition. Toner's continuum theory, developed with Yuhai Tu, showed that long-range orientational order survives in two dimensions because nonlinear fluctuations evade the Mermin-Wagner restriction. Ramaswamy and collaborators built the hydrodynamics of active suspensions, with giant number fluctuations and anomalous scaling. The three credited names map onto three distinct, identifiable contributions. The field is more than three decades old and has been tested quantitatively in bacterial suspensions, cytoskeletal gels, vibrated granular matter and synthetic colloids. The concept is general and not tied to any one material, which I consider the best sign of a lasting physics contribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Yuhai Tu is a co-author of the Toner-Tu theory and cannot be named within the supplied credit, and early work by Simha and Ramaswamy and by Marchetti and colleagues is also left out. A prize to these three would be defensible, but it would be incomplete. The second reservation is that the exactness of the Toner-Tu scaling exponents in two dimensions is still contested experimentally, so some colleagues may see the core quantitative prediction as not fully confirmed. Third, the headline experimental realisations lie close to biology and soft matter, and the committee would have to argue that this is physics of general importance. Finally, my first-place ranking is not shared by any other member. That is a real fact about the opening ballots and should not be read as support.

responses.point: Pearce ranks Kane, Mele and Molenkamp first because the Z2 and quantum spin Hall prediction and its HgTe realisation opened a class of materials, with more than fifteen years of independent confirmation.
responses.response: I agree with Pearce on maturity and that the idea-to-experiment chain is clean; I ranked this fourth and it has the broadest support in the room. I disagree that the attribution is as settled as he suggests. His own ballot concedes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route, Zhang is deceased, and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan sits outside the trio. The Molenkamp share is therefore tied to a prediction made by people who cannot be named. That is no weaker than the attribution problem in my own preferred candidate, so I do not accept that it favours B042 over B005. It does make B042 the strongest fallback in my view, because the field's maturity is not in doubt.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's record-accuracy realisation define a clean two-person prize with good maturity, and she regards it as perhaps overdue given the 2005 and 2012 prizes on adjacent topics.
responses.response: I accept that the attribution is the cleanest on the table, and that multiple laboratories have reproduced the 1e-18-class performance. I rank it fifth because I see it as an advance in measurement. I question 'overdue'. Kroll, in his own opening statement, concedes that the frequency comb and ion clocks have already been recognised and that some members may see the lattice clock as incremental. The redefinition of the second has also not happened. I would want the committee to say what new physical principle the clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength trick, since the Statutes reward a discovery or invention of importance and do not reward the sharpest instrument. I would not block it, which is why it stays among my alternatives.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs observation first, as the experimental completion of the electroweak sector that has no prize since the 2013 theory award, while admitting the credit problem.
responses.response: I agree that the physics is of the first rank. My difficulty is practical. As Danielsson himself says, three founding leaders cannot represent two collaborations of thousands, and the supplied names are proxies chosen by role rather than by decisive discovery contributions. Pearce says the same in his own assessment. Any prize here would be arbitrary in a way I cannot defend to the wider community. The discovery is not in doubt, but the person-based prize may be unworkable. I would therefore not put B006 in my preferred configuration unless a principled and defensible three-person credit rule is shown. I would like to hear from Danielsson whether he has such a rule.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a concrete instrumentation breakthrough and also ranks circuit QED and the Cirac-Zoller proposals highly, while noting the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize.
responses.response: Kroll's own caveat about overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the point on which I rely, and I take it seriously. I note that his top three are all in atomic, optical and quantum-information physics, and the same is true of Johansson's and Danielsson's. If we pick one of these, the committee should be clear that we have chosen the most mature item in a crowded neighbourhood of AMO work already recognised in 2005, 2012 and 2022, and not the only candidate. Statistical physics has never had a prize for nonequilibrium collective phenomena of this kind, so B005 does not compete with prior prizes.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a prize that omits Yuhai Tu from the Toner-Tu theory, given the three-person limit.

Whether the exact two-dimensional Toner-Tu exponents are experimentally established well enough, or whether the prize should rest on the existence of the flocking phase and the hydrodynamic framework only.
Whether active matter will be judged as physics of sufficiently general importance, since the best-known experimental realisations are biological or soft-matter systems.
How much weight to give a candidate that only I ranked first, when B042 has much broader opening support.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from the provided profile. Active matter and stochastic dynamics lie close to my own research interests, but none of Toner, Ramaswamy or Vicsek appears among my documented co-authors or institutional connections, and I rely on the supplied evidence without claiming any undocumented relationship. The subject proximity should be discounted accordingly.
